Honour, Disgrace to Displacement: Nautch Girls in Colonial India

Abstract:

In Indian cultural and performative traditions, hereditary dancers such as devadasis and tawaifs held a significant position for their command over music, dance, and other artistic skills. In colonial literature, the usage of the term &ldquonautch girl&rdquo or &ldquodancing girl&rdquo referred to these elite performers systematically erasing their distinct cultural identities. &ldquoNautch&rdquo increasingly conflated with the label &ldquoprostitute&rdquo for the unique sexual relationship that courtesans and devadasis had with their patrons. This thesis explores how, in the second half of the nineteenth century, the identity of nautch girls underwent significant changes. It helped colonial rulers to exert greater control over their sexuality and socio-economic position within Indian society by incorporating legal, medical and moral discourses. Further, the perceived sexual deviancy of nautch girls that allowed them to form amorous relationships with the British soldiers and officers made them sexual rivals of the memsahibs. This thesis unravels how this sexual rivalry between the women of the two races was integrated by the colonial rulers in a system of hierarchy to promote racial superiority, making the memsahibs active agents in limiting the position of nautch girls further. Besides controlling the &ldquobodies&rdquo of nautch girls, demand for their displacement from urban spaces was put forward jointly by educated Indians and Christian missionaries through the Anti-nautch Movement. Based on a qualitative and exploratory methodology, this thesis draws upon colonial archives, reformist writings, and select Anglo-Indian fictional texts of the nineteenth century to interrogate how literature propagated and reinstated the colonial perception regarding nautch girls. The study argues that colonial literary discourse played a decisive role in reinforcing colonial mechanisms of control, surveillance and displacement by recasting the female hereditary dancers within the frameworks of social disorder and moral deviance in nineteenth century India.

Keywords: Nautch Girls, Colonisers, Memsahibs, Anti-nautch Movement, Anglo-Indian Fictions
